The full recommendations were not read.

How each response moves her rapport and readiness, and the rule that her old full program or a daily catch-up schedule after six weeks off brings on exertional rhabdomyolysis on day 2, are authored. The direction follows the CSCCa and NSCA guidance: a novel or full-volume workload after detraining is the classic setting for exertional rhabdomyolysis, and volume is cut by about half in the first week back. writeup.question: For her record: what caused the lapse, how you built the plan back, and how you kept her safe and training.

parts.label: The lapse
parts.criteria: Names the barriers (caregiving, shifts) in her words, without blame; treats the lapse as expected, not a failure.
parts.modelAnswer: Six weeks off while caring for her mother after hip surgery and with new shifts; she felt she had failed. I treated it as a normal lapse and explored it without blame.

parts.label: The plan back
parts.criteria: No 'making up': activity is spread across the week (150-300 min, strength twice a week); after six weeks off, about half the old volume with lighter loads, built up over weeks; an if-then fallback for the next disruption.
parts.modelAnswer: No catch-up: the guidelines spread activity over the week. After six weeks off she starts at about half her old volume, twice a week, building over four weeks, with a 10-minute fallback when her mother needs her.

parts.label: Safety
parts.criteria: Self-monitoring with the warning signs; severe muscle pain or swelling with dark urine after training means stop and get medical care the same day (possible exertional rhabdomyolysis), not 'train through it'.
parts.modelAnswer: She logs effort and knows to report severe pain, swelling, weakness or dark urine at once; those mean medical care today, not more training.

expertPath.text: Ask what got in the way and listen; affirm that coming back counts.
Explain that activity adds up across the week and cannot be made up in one day; write a re-entry plan at about half her old volume.

back.headline: Back, and staying
back.body: No blame, a plan built for her real week, a gentle restart and a fallback for the next disruption. That is how a lapse stays a lapse.

gaps.headline: Back, with gaps
gaps.body: Look at the load (half her old volume after six weeks off, never a catch-up), the words (barriers, not blame) and the plan for the next disruption.

quit.headline: The lapse became an exit
quit.body: Blame turned a lapse into a reason to leave. Ask what got in the way; affirm the return.

trainedThrough.headline: Dark urine is not soreness
trainedThrough.body: Severe pain and swelling with cola-colored urine after a hard return is a warning of exertional rhabdomyolysis: stop and get medical care the same day.

unanswered.headline: Answer the warning sign
unanswered.body: Severe pain, swelling and dark urine after training need medical care today.

scoring.modelReasoning: A lapse is expected, not a failure: explore the barriers (caregiving, new shifts) without blame and affirm the return. Activity counts across the week (150-300 minutes, strength twice a week) and cannot be made up in a day. After six weeks off, restart at about half the old volume and build over weeks; a novel or full workload after detraining is the classic setting for exertional rhabdomyolysis. Plan the next disruption (if-then, a 10-minute fallback), teach self-monitoring and the warning signs, and send dark urine with severe muscle pain to medical care the same day.
